title: Clement of Rome
hook: a letter from Rome to quarreling Corinth: be humble, be at peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Didache, a handbook for beginners, and your line was two ways.

The church in Corinth has pushed out its leaders. Not for stealing, not for false teaching. A few bold people stirred things up, and elders who had served well were removed. The news travels across the sea to Rome, and the church there writes back: a long letter, patient and firm, from the church of God sojourning at Rome to the church sojourning at Corinth. It never signs a personal name. But tradition names the one who held the pen: Clement, a leader of the Roman church. And Corinth, it turns out, had been here before.

Clement reminds them: take up the letter of the blessed Paul. Years earlier Paul had written to this same church about the same problem: "every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ." Different camps, same quarrel. Clement's medicine is humility. He quotes the old proverb that also appears in the Letter of James: "God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble." He fills page after page with examples from the scriptures of people who were lowly and lifted up, and of jealousy that destroyed people, from Cain onward. He reaches for Peter and Paul too, examples from his own generation who suffered through jealousy and strife. Then he writes a hymn to love, close to Paul's own: love makes no divisions, love stirs up no rebellion, love does all things in harmony. Then he asks something remarkable of the people who started the trouble. Whoever is noble among you, he writes, let him say: if this fight is because of me, I'll leave; I'll go wherever you want; only let the flock of Christ be at peace with its elders. Not throw them out. Invite them to step down on their own. Paul had told the Philippians the same: "in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves." Catholic tradition counts Clement among the early bishops of Rome. His message for Corinth: let the proud be humbled, and let the flock be at peace.
screen: `I AM OF PAUL; AND I OF APOLLOS.`
`IF IT'S BECAUSE OF ME, I'LL GO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one strained relationship, a friend, a sibling, a coworker, someone in a group you belong to, and ask Clement's hard question quietly: how much of this is because of me? In your head, put your own share into three plain sentences, with no blame and no arguing their side for them; you don't have to send anything. If you pray, hold that person before God.
Clement. The leader tradition names as the writer of the Roman church's letter to quarreling Corinth: be humble, and be at peace.
Your line: let the proud be humbled. Humility was Clement's medicine for a church at odds. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Clement's letter is read today among the writings of the Apostolic Fathers, and the Catholic Church remembers Clement as a saint and an early bishop of Rome.

Throw the troublemakers out at once and appoint stronger new leaders.
Split into two churches so each side could keep its own leaders.
chat.meaning: Clement's medicine was humility. He asked the ones who stirred things up to step down on their own, so the flock could be at peace with its elders.
